meta.title: Romanian C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1,500 more words, none of them in A1 to B2 · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Romanian → English (see the Romanian, recall the meaning) and English → Romanian (see an English meaning, recall the Romanian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be — no openly licensed graded word list for Romanian was found to build it from. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 544 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — economics and finance, politics and the state, law and rights, science and knowledge, philosophy, language and rhetoric, society and culture, character and conduct, the finer shades of feeling, the arts and literature, the planet, medicine, the adjectives, adverbs and connectors of a formal register, nuanced verbs, and abstract nouns — and the other 956 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Romanian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword carries its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own, because Romanian does not write where the stress falls. Verbs are given in the dictionary's form, with the infinitive's a (a face, to do). The 905 nouns show their gender — masculine, feminine or neuter, the neuter being masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural — their plural, and their definite form, the article being a suffix (casă, a house; casa, the house); the 274 verbs show their first person, past participle and subjunctive, and behind the All forms fold their present, imperfect, subjunctive and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 771 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 308 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

Sindromul Paris este un fel de șoc cultural. Este un termen psihiatric folosit pentru a descrie străinii care încep să trăiască la Paris, care atrași de imaginea orașului de centru al modei, nu se adaptează bine la obiceiurile și cultura locală, își pierd echilibrul mental și prezintă simptome similare cu cele ale depresiei.
The Paris syndrome is a type of culture shock. It's a psychiatric term used to describe foreigners who start living in Paris, drawn to the image of the city as a center of fashion, don't adapt well to the local customs and culture, lose their mental balance and exhibit symptoms close to depression.
Sindroamele sunt adesea denumite după medicul sau grupul de medici care le-a descoperit sau care a descris inițial tabloul clinic complet. Astfel de nume de sindroame eponime sunt exemple de eponime medicale. Recent, a existat o schimbare în direcția denumirii descriptive a afecțiunilor (după simptome sau cauza care stă la baza acestora) mai degrabă decât a denumirii eponime, dar denumirile eponime ale sindroamelor persistă adesea în uzul comun.
Syndromes are often named after the physician or group of physicians who discovered them or initially described the full clinical picture. Such eponymous syndrome names are examples of medical eponyms. Recently, there has been a shift towards naming conditions descriptively (by symptoms or underlying cause) rather than eponymously, but the eponymous syndrome names often persist in common usage.
